turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. It's really nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I, um... I hope I'm not wasting your time, but I've just been having a little trouble at work lately. Nothing awful, I promise, just... well, what finally pushed me to make an appointment is that I'll start an EPIC quality report, or I'll sit down in one of our clinic metrics meetings, and I have every intention of tracking everything perfectly. 

But... within just a few minutes, my mind just sort of drifts. It drifts so far that I find myself rereading the exact same numbers over and over, or I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. It's a bit embarrassing to admit, honestly, especially at my age and in my position. I mean, it's probably just normal stress from managing the clinic, right? Does that make sense... like, is that a valid reason to come see you?

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention during tasks like reading reports or attending meetings, noting that their mind drifts within minutes.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your life, did you experience these kinds of difficulties with focus and concentration when you were in grade school, or is this a relatively new experience for you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, um... I guess if I really think about it, it's not entirely new. But I want to be clear, I wasn't a bad student or anything! I always tried really hard to do well. It's just... even back in elementary school, I remember my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright, but, well, maybe a little careless. Just silly mistakes, you know? 

And my mother, bless her heart, she actually had to sit right next to me at the kitchen table while I finished my homework. If she didn't, I would just sort of... lose track of the assignments, or I'd realize I completely forgot to bring my books home from school. But I did always get it done with her help! I hope that doesn't make me sound horribly irresponsible... is that the kind of information you're looking for?

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports that teachers noted they were 'careless' and made 'silly mistakes' in elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient required their mother to sit with them to finish homework, otherwise they would lose track of assignments, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions frequently forgetting to bring necessary books home from school.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of these difficulties with focus, do you often find yourself feeling restless, keyed up, or unable to stop worrying about everyday events or potential problems in your life?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, I wouldn't say I feel restless or keyed up. I mean, I worry about things sometimes, just like anyone else, I suppose—wanting to make sure the clinic runs smoothly, wanting to do a good job for the doctors and the staff. But I don't feel like I can't stop worrying, and I certainly don't feel jittery or on edge. 

I really try to keep a positive outlook and not let things get to me too much. I hope that's a good thing? I just... I don't want to give you the impression that I'm some sort of nervous wreck. I'm actually generally pretty calm, it's just this silly trouble with paying attention to the details sometimes. Does that answer your question okay?

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient mentions having 'trouble with paying attention to the details sometimes.'
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient states they worry like anyone else but are generally pretty calm and not a 'nervous wreck,' denying excessive worry.
symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient explicitly states, 'I don't feel like I can't stop worrying.'
symptom_reasoning.S058: The patient explicitly denies feeling restless, keyed up, jittery, or on edge.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often find yourself frequently interrupting others when they are speaking or struggling to wait your turn in conversations or group settings?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no. I really try my best to be polite and listen to people. In my role at the clinic, it's so important to hear everyone out, you know? I would feel just terrible if I was constantly talking over people or cutting them off. 

I mean, I suppose everyone gets excited and jumps in occasionally, but I really don't think I do that very often. I'm usually the one sitting quietly in the meetings... maybe drifting off a bit, like I mentioned, but definitely not interrupting! I always try to wait for my turn to speak. I hope that's the right answer? I just wouldn't want you to think I was rude or anything like that.

symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly states they always try to wait for their turn to speak.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting others, stating they would feel terrible talking over people or cutting them off.

turns.doctor_question: When you are sitting in those long meetings where you find your mind drifting, do you find yourself feeling the need to constantly fidget, tap your feet, or move around in your chair?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, definitely not. I really make a point to maintain a professional composure during those meetings. It would just be so disrespectful to the doctors and the board members if I were squirming around or tapping my pen, you know? So I sit very still. 

Even if my mind is... well, maybe wandering a little bit like we talked about, physically I'm very quiet. I would absolutely hate to draw any negative attention to myself or disrupt someone's presentation. I just try to look attentive, even if I'm having a little trouble staying focused on the actual words. Is that... is that normal? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient acknowledges having trouble staying focused on the actual words during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies squirming, tapping, or fidgeting, stating they sit very still to maintain professional composure.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your trouble with focus in meetings, do you find that you frequently lose important items like your keys, phone, or paperwork, or struggle to keep your personal or work space organized?
turns.patient_response:
Oh... well... I try so hard to keep everything perfectly organized, I really do. But... I suppose, if I'm being completely honest, I have been misplacing a few things lately. It's actually a bit embarrassing to admit. 

I just... I find myself constantly hunting for my clinic badge, or my handwritten notes... sometimes even clinic folders or the flash drive I literally just had in my hand right before a meeting. I don't want you to think my office is a disaster area, because I really do try to keep it looking professional! It's just... I used to be the organized one, you know? The one everyone relied on to have everything together. And now I'm the one scrambling to find my own notes. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound incompetent? I really am trying my absolute best to stay on top of it all, I promise. I just don't know why I keep setting things down and forgetting where they went. Is that... is that helpful for what you're looking for?

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they are constantly hunting for misplaced items like their clinic badge, handwritten notes, folders, and flash drives.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself frequently delaying or avoiding starting tasks that require a significant amount of mental effort, such as completing those quality reports or reviewing complex paperwork?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... well, I really do pride myself on getting all my work done. I always make sure everything is finished by the end of the day, I promise you that. 

But... I guess, if I'm thinking about those really dense policy reviews, or the long blocks of data analysis... I might, um, sort of push those to the late afternoon? It's just that the thought of sitting down with all that heavy, detailed reading and... and all that intense thinking... it almost feels physically hard to just start it, if that makes sense? 

I don't mean to sound lazy! I'm definitely not lazy. I just... I find myself doing all the smaller, easier tasks first, and then I realize I've put off the big reports until the very end of the day. I still get them done, though! I hope that's okay? I just want to be honest with you, even if it doesn't sound very good. Does that make sense for what you're asking?

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient admits to delaying dense policy reviews and data analysis because the intense thinking required feels physically hard to start.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states they always make sure everything is finished by the end of the day, denying a failure to finish workplace duties.

turns.doctor_question: When you are trying to work on those important reports, do you find that you are easily distracted by noises or other things happening around your office, such as people talking nearby or emails popping up on your screen?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, actually... no, I don't really think I struggle with that part. I'm usually pretty good at tuning out the background noise. I mean, managing a busy clinic, there are always staff talking in the halls or phones ringing, but I really make an effort to just keep my head down and stay glued to my screen. And with emails... well, I just ignore the little pop-ups until I'm at a good stopping point. 

I hope that doesn't sound like I'm contradicting what I said earlier about my focus? I just... I really don't want you to think I'm sitting there staring out the open door at every little thing that walks by. I promise I'm very dedicated to my work once I actually get myself to sit down and do it. Does that... does that make sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you an accurate picture of how I work.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they do not struggle with being distracted by background noise or emails, and are good at tuning them out.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find that you often struggle to follow through on instructions or finish projects or tasks that you have started, even when you understand what needs to be done?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... well, I really try to be thorough. I always write down what needs to be done, and I make a genuine effort to get every step completed. I don't want you to think I just abandon my responsibilities or ignore people's requests. 

But... I suppose, if I'm looking at it critically... sometimes, if someone gives me, say, three or four follow-up steps after a committee meeting... I'll jump right in and do the first one immediately. And I'll usually start drafting the second one, too! But then... I don't know, somehow the email, or the spreadsheet, or the final submission just sort of... sits there unfinished. Usually until someone gently reminds me about it. 

I feel so terrible when that happens. It's not that I don't understand the instructions, or that I don't care! I really do care. I just... I somehow lose the thread of it before I can cross the finish line. I always get it done eventually, though, once they remind me! I hope that doesn't make me sound unreliable? I really am trying to be better about following through all the way. Is that the kind of example you were looking for?

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient confirms that despite starting tasks and understanding instructions, they often leave steps unfinished until reminded, indicating difficulty following through.
